case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment permits Congress to categorically disarm a person who is an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), at least as applied to a habitual drug user who possessed a firearm while not necessarily intoxicated.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (firearm possession ban for anyone who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”), challenged under the Second Amendment (as interpreted through the text-and-history framework of New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because historical firearm regulations support disarming individuals whose ongoing conduct and condition make them dangerous or unreliable with arms—particularly laws restricting weapon possession/use by the intoxicated and those suffering from mental illness or otherwise posing heightened risk. The government contends that habitual unlawful drug use is a relevantly similar risk category to historically regulated groups, and that Bruen allows modern regulations that are analogous in purpose and burden even if not identical in founding-era form. The petitioner also emphasizes the practical and institutional stakes: § 922(g)(3) is frequently used in federal prosecutions, and the Fifth Circuit’s decision invalidated most applications, creating (and deepening) a circuit split that warrants Supreme Court correction.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues that § 922(g)(3), as applied, violates the Second Amendment under Bruen because the government cannot identify a sufficiently close historical analogue for a broad, status-based prohibition on gun possession by people who use illegal drugs, especially when the person is not shown to be intoxicated or actively impaired at the time of possession. In respondent’s view, founding-era and Reconstruction-era laws focused on disarming specific dangerous persons (often tied to concrete threats, misconduct, or active intoxication) rather than imposing an ongoing ban based on prior or habitual drug use. Respondent also points to inconsistent lower-court outcomes after Bruen as evidence that the government’s proffered analogies are too general, and that the Fifth Circuit correctly applied Bruen’s demand for historically grounded limits on disarmament.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen (2022)
United States v. Harris (3d Cir. 2025) (as referenced in the petitioner’s reply brief)
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va. 2023), aff’d (4th Cir. 2025), cert. denied (2025) (discussed in amici materials as an example of Bruen-era methodological difficulty)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Thomas press the most serious objection: the government’s analogues largely regulate armed conduct while actively intoxicated (or impose individualized surety requirements), whereas § 922(g)(3) can reach possession during sober intervals based on a potentially elastic status label. But under Rahimi’s “why/how” framework—emphasized by Justice Kavanaugh—the absence of a founding-era twin is not dispositive if the restriction is comparably justified and comparably burdensome, and the way to respect the temporal limits of the historical tradition is to construe “unlawful user” narrowly to require contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use closely connected to the time of possession. Justice Gorsuch’s indeterminacy/lenity concern does not compel facial invalidation; it reinforces the need for a constrained, as-applied reversal that rejects remote or sporadic use and avoids an open-ended dangerousness power while preserving administrable enforcement. Heller’s “presumptively lawful” passage cannot do the historical work alone, but it supports the premise that categorical prohibitions are not per se unconstitutional, making a narrow disposition institutionally appropriate.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is that Rahimi permits disarming risk-defined “categories” and that we can save § 922(g)(3) by construing “unlawful user” to mean contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual use. But Rahimi did not dilute Bruen’s requirement that the Government identify a historical tradition supporting a comparably justified and comparably burdensome restriction; the intoxication analogues regulate armed conduct during active impairment, not a continuing possession ban reaching sober intervals. Nor can we adopt Roberts’s narrowing construction when it is not anchored in the statutory text—Justice Gorsuch is right that indeterminacy and lenity concerns underscore that courts may not rewrite “unlawful user” into a temporally precise standard to supply the missing historical fit. Heller’s “presumptively lawful” dictum, invoked by Justices Alito and Kavanaugh, cannot do the historical work Bruen demands for this particular prohibition, so the Government has not carried its burden as applied here.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s temporal-mismatch objection is the most serious: founding-era rules largely targeted being armed while actively intoxicated, whereas § 922(g)(3) can extend into sober intervals. But under Bruen as clarified by Rahimi, the government need not produce a dead-ringer; the question is whether the restriction is relevantly similar in “why” (preventing dangerous armed misuse tied to a recurring impairment condition) and “how” (a temporary disarmament keyed to a contemporaneous, ongoing condition). Chief Justice Roberts’s narrowing construction—treating “unlawful user” as requiring contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use close in time to possession—meaningfully answers both Justice Gorsuch’s lenity/fair-notice concern and Justice Thomas’s worry about an indeterminate, free-floating status ban by keeping the statute tethered to a concrete, administrable risk state rather than remote history or sporadic use. On that limited, as-applied understanding, the Fifth Circuit’s broad invalidation demands too exact a historical match and undervalues the practical consequences for enforceability and public safety that Rahimi recognizes legislatures may address through risk-defined categories.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is the “how” mismatch: founding-era intoxication rules were keyed to actual impairment, while § 922(g)(3) risks operating as a broader status ban reaching sober possession. But under Rahimi’s why/how framework—as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes—the absence of a founding-era twin is not dispositive if the modern law, properly construed, targets the same danger (armed misuse during a recurrent impairment condition) with a comparably limited burden. I agree with Roberts and Justice Kagan that the constitutionally sound path is a narrow, as-applied understanding of “unlawful user” requiring contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use closely connected to possession, which also answers Gorsuch’s fair-notice/lenity concern by reducing prosecutorial discretion and avoiding moment-of-intoxication mini-trials. That approach preserves access to justice and protects public safety without endorsing a free-floating dangerousness rationale untethered to history.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point is the “how” mismatch: founding-era analogues generally target being armed while actually intoxicated, while § 922(g)(3) can reach possession during sober intervals. But I think the Chief Justice is right that the statute’s text can bear (and constitutional avoidance favors) a narrowing construction of “unlawful user” to require contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use closely connected in time to possession—so the burden operates like an extended impairment/risk condition rather than a remote status disability. Under Rahimi’s why/how framework (as Justice Kavanaugh stresses), that narrowed application fits the historical tradition of temporarily disabling arms possession for risk-laden conditions, even if no founding-era law is a perfect twin. Barrett’s worry that narrowing is extra-textual doesn’t carry the day for me because “user” is naturally usage-based and temporally anchored, and reading it to include sporadic or stale use would create the very indeterminacy and overbreadth Gorsuch identifies—making the narrower reading the more coherent, workable textual construction.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s proposed narrowing construction (and Justice Kavanaugh’s similar approach) meaningfully mitigates my fair-notice/lenity concern by tightening “unlawful user” to contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual use, but it does not satisfy Bruen/Rahimi’s historical-tradition demand. As Justice Barrett stresses, the founding-era intoxication analogues chiefly regulated armed conduct while actually impaired, and the surety/peace-bond tradition required a concrete, individualized showing—not a categorical disability that continues through sober intervals based on an elastic status label. Rahimi’s “why/how” framework does not authorize a free-floating dangerousness power to uphold modern status prohibitions absent a relevantly similar historical mechanism for disarmament, and Heller’s “presumptively lawful” dictum (invoked by Justices Alito and Kavanaugh) cannot do the government’s historical work. Given that mismatch in the “how,” I would affirm the as-applied judgment for Respondent on this record rather than rewriting the statute to reach a constitutional result.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch press the best point: the founding-era intoxication laws were tethered to actual impairment, while § 922(g)(3) can extend into sober intervals, creating a serious “how” mismatch under Bruen. But Chief Justice Roberts is right that Rahimi’s why/how framework does not demand a dead-ringer, and it supports disarming a defined category when the justification is the same kind of misuse risk and the burden is comparable—so long as we avoid an untethered dangerousness power. The way to meet that objection, and to address Justice Gorsuch’s fair-notice/lenity concern without rewriting the statute, is a narrowing construction that treats “unlawful user” as contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use closely connected in time to possession—functionally an extended impairment condition rather than a remote status disability. On that understanding, the Fifth Circuit’s categorical invalidation goes too far, and reversal on a limited, as-applied basis better fits history, precedent, and institutional administrability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh make the best case that Rahimi permits categorical disarmament keyed to dangerousness and that we can construe “unlawful user” to mean contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual use close in time to possession. Even with that narrowing gloss, however, the Government still has not identified a founding-era tradition imposing a comparable burden—disarmament during sober intervals based on a status label—rather than regulating contemporaneous intoxicated carrying or using individualized tools like surety/peace bonds tied to a concrete threat, as Justice Gorsuch emphasizes. Rahimi’s “why/how” inquiry cannot be satisfied by administrability alone: the “how” here remains materially broader in temporal scope than the analogues offered, and Heller’s “presumptively lawful” dictum (invoked by Justice Alito) cannot do the historical work Bruen requires for this specific restriction. On this record, I would not reverse the Fifth Circuit’s as-applied Second Amendment holding.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Gorsuch’s core objection—the founding-era intoxication laws were keyed to being armed while actually impaired, while § 922(g)(3) can reach sober intervals—remains the hardest “how” problem under Bruen/Rahimi. But I think the Chief Justice is right that Rahimi does not force courts into individualized, moment-by-moment dangerousness findings; it permits legislatures to address a demonstrated risk through administrable category rules, so long as the burden is comparably justified and bounded. The way to respect Barrett’s temporal-mismatch concern without creating Gorsuch’s fair-notice/lenity morass is a narrow construction (as Roberts and Justice Kagan suggest) requiring contemporaneous, ongoing, habitual unlawful use closely connected in time to possession—making the prohibition operate like an extended impairment-risk condition rather than a free-floating status ban. On that as-applied footing, the Fifth Circuit’s intoxication-at-the-moment demand would yield arbitrary impairment mini-trials and uneven enforcement, which Rahimi’s pragmatics counsel against.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen’s text-and-history framework, the government may disarm categories of persons shown by historical tradition to present an unusual risk to themselves or others, and Rahimi confirms that legislatures may impose firearms restrictions tied to dangerousness without requiring a freewheeling, case-by-case adjudication of risk in every prosecution. Section 922(g)(3) is best understood—and should be upheld on narrow, as-applied grounds here—as targeting ongoing, habitual unlawful drug use that makes firearm possession more dangerous and unreliable, analogous in principle to historical regulations restricting armed conduct by the intoxicated and other persons whose condition rendered firearm use especially hazardous. A categorical rule also avoids the administrability, notice, and institutional problems of requiring courts to litigate individualized “dangerousness” determinations in routine prosecutions, a concern this Court has recognized in other contexts. Respect for precedent and institutional stability counsels reversing the Fifth Circuit’s broad invalidation and sustaining § 922(g)(3) at least as applied to a habitual user possessing a firearm during the period of ongoing unlawful use.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s text-and-history framework, the Second Amendment’s plain text presumptively covers an ordinary citizen’s possession of a firearm, so the Government bears the burden to justify § 922(g)(3) by historical tradition. The founding-era and Reconstruction-era record reflects narrow, conduct-based restrictions—e.g., punishing carrying or firing while actively intoxicated or using surety/peace-bond regimes tied to concrete threats—not a categorical, status-based disarmament of anyone deemed an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances regardless of intoxication at the time of possession, as § 922(g)(3) imposes. Heller’s assurance about “longstanding prohibitions” cannot supply the missing historical analogue here, and Bruen (as reaffirmed by Rahimi’s “why/how” test) requires more than generalized appeals to dangerousness. Because § 922(g)(3) is a broad federal ban untethered to contemporaneous impairment or individualized findings, it exceeds the historically understood limits on disarmament and is unconstitutional as applied.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: As applied to a habitual unlawful drug user, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within the Second Amendment’s historically recognized power to disarm categories of persons whose ongoing condition makes them dangerous or unreliable with arms, even if the individual was not provably intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Heller emphasized that the right is not unlimited and identified “presumptively lawful” prohibitions on possession by certain categories (including felons and the mentally ill), and Bruen’s text-and-history test does not require a dead-ringer founding-era statute so long as the modern regulation is relevantly similar in purpose and burden. Historical restrictions on carrying or using firearms while intoxicated, along with analogous traditions of disarming those deemed dangerous, support Congress’s judgment that habitual unlawful drug use correlates with heightened risk and warrants categorical disarmament. Given the practical consequences and law-enforcement reliance on § 922(g)(3), the Fifth Circuit’s near-categorical invalidation should be reversed.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As applied to a habitual unlawful drug user, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within the Second Amendment’s historically recognized power to disarm categories of persons who pose a heightened risk of dangerous gun misuse. Under Bruen’s text-and-history method, the government need not produce a founding-era statute identical in form; it need only show a relevantly similar tradition in purpose and burden, and historical restrictions on the armed intoxicated and other risk-laden conditions provide that analogue even when the person is not intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Rahimi confirms that legislatures may temporarily disarm “categories of persons” who present a “special danger of misuse,” and that inquiry is more administrable and historically grounded than an overbroad “responsible citizen” limitation rejected there. Given the real-world stakes for public safety and vulnerable communities affected by gun violence, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) at least as applied to habitual users whose ongoing unlawful use creates a sustained risk profile akin to historically regulated dangerousness categories.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen, the government must show that § 922(g)(3)’s restriction is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition by identifying a relevantly similar analogue in terms of both “why” and “how” it burdens the right. While founding-era law may not contain an identical, status-based ban keyed to “unlawful user,” history does support disarming or restricting arms for categories of persons whose condition or ongoing conduct makes firearms possession especially dangerous or unreliable (e.g., restrictions tied to intoxication and other risk-based incapacities), which is sufficiently analogous in justification and burden when applied to a habitual, contemporaneous drug user. Reading § 922(g)(3) as targeting current, ongoing unlawful use (not remote past use) also makes the statute more coherent and workable, and avoids the Fifth Circuit’s near-categorical invalidation that would substantially disrupt longstanding federal enforcement. Heller’s assurance that “longstanding prohibitions” on firearm possession by certain categories are presumptively lawful reinforces sustaining Congress’s judgment here, at least as applied to habitual users possessing during the period of use.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers keeping and bearing arms, the government must justify § 922(g)(3) by pointing to a well-established historical analogue. The proffered intoxication laws regulated carrying or firing weapons while actively impaired, not a categorical, status-based, ongoing disarmament of a person who uses drugs at other times; that mismatch in burden and justification fails Bruen’s “relevantly similar” inquiry. Nor does Heller’s reference to “presumptively lawful” regulations supply an atextual carveout broad enough to sustain § 922(g)(3) as applied to a person possessing a firearm while not intoxicated, and any ambiguity in a criminal prohibition that turns on an indeterminate status like “unlawful user” counsels restraint under the rule of lenity. Respect for separation of powers reinforces the same conclusion: if Congress wishes to disarm based on demonstrated dangerousness, it must do so within constitutional limits grounded in the Nation’s historical tradition, not by expanding a categorical prohibition beyond any clear historical counterpart.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen, the government must show § 922(g)(3) is consistent with our historical tradition, and history supports disarming categories of persons who pose special dangers of misuse, not only through individualized judgments. Heller’s discussion of “longstanding prohibitions on the possession of firearms by felons and the mentally ill” as “presumptively lawful” indicates that categorical, status-based disarmament can be constitutional when tied to a danger/unreliability rationale, and my Bruen concurrence emphasized that point. Applying that framework here, habitual unlawful drug use is sufficiently analogous to historically regulated conditions like intoxication-based arms restrictions and other danger-based incapacities, making § 922(g)(3) constitutional at least as applied to a habitual user even if not shown intoxicated at the precise moment of possession. Given the statute’s workability and the institutional need for a clear rule (and to resolve post-Bruen disuniformity), I would reverse the Fifth Circuit and uphold the statute as applied.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s text covers the conduct (keeping a firearm), the Government must justify § 922(g)(3) by showing a relevantly similar historical analogue as to both the law’s “why” and “how.” Founding- and Reconstruction-era laws cited by the Government largely addressed contemporaneous impairment (e.g., using/carrying firearms while intoxicated) or individualized determinations of dangerousness, not a categorical, status-based disarmament that persists during sober intervals based on being an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3). Heller’s reference to “presumptively lawful” regulations does not supply the required historical demonstration for this specific prohibition, and the analogy to intoxication statutes is materially mismatched in temporal scope and burden. Because the Government has not carried its burden to show a historical tradition supporting this breadth of disarmament as applied to a habitual user not shown to be intoxicated at the time of possession, I would affirm the Second Amendment challenge in this posture.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: As applied to a habitual unlawful drug user, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within Bruen’s allowance for modern regulations that are relevantly analogous in purpose and burden to historical limits aimed at preventing gun violence by persons whose condition makes them dangerous or unreliable with arms. Consistent with Rahimi’s emphasis that legislatures may disarm categories of persons tied to demonstrated risk (without forcing courts into unadministrable, case-by-case “dangerousness” mini-trials), Congress may treat ongoing unlawful drug use as a status closely connected to impairment and heightened misuse risk, akin to historical restrictions on the intoxicated and other dangerous conditions. Heller also recognized that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and tolerates longstanding disarmament measures, supporting the constitutionality of targeted prohibitions like § 922(g)(3). Requiring individualized proof that the defendant was intoxicated at the moment of possession would undermine procedural fairness and administrability, inviting arbitrary outcomes and extensive litigation over contested impairment metrics rather than enforcing a clear, predictable rule.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the Second Amendment permits Congress to categorically bar firearm possession by a person who is an “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances under 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), at least as applied to Ali Danial Hemani.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) (prohibiting firearm possession by any person who “is an unlawful user of or addicted to any controlled substance”); U.S. Const. amend. II; the interpretive framework from New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(3) is constitutional as applied because historical tradition supports disarming categories of persons whose condition or behavior makes them dangerous or unreliable with arms, and because founding-era and 19th-century analogues (notably restrictions on carrying/using firearms while intoxicated and regulations aimed at dangerousness) are sufficiently similar under Bruen’s analogical method. The government also stresses that the Fifth Circuit’s ruling effectively invalidates most applications of an important, frequently used federal statute, deepens an acknowledged circuit conflict, and should be reversed to restore consistent enforcement of gun prohibitions for active/habitual unlawful drug users even when they are not proven to be intoxicated at the precise moment of possession.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Hemani argues that § 922(g)(3), as applied to him, violates the Second Amendment under Bruen because the government cannot identify a well-established historical tradition of permanently or categorically disarming people solely for being unlawful drug users (as opposed to disarming people actively intoxicated or otherwise shown to be presently dangerous). In his view, historical laws cited by the government—especially intoxication-related restrictions—do not justify a broad status-based ban untethered to contemporaneous impairment, individualized dangerousness, or a comparable founding-era practice; therefore, the Fifth Circuit was right to hold the statute unconstitutional in most applications and to reject the government’s analogies.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Ass’n v. Bruen
United States v. Harris (3d Cir. 2025) (mentioned as deepening the circuit conflict)
United States v. Hill (E.D. Va. 2023), aff’d (4th Cir. 2025), cert. denied (2025) (mentioned re Bruen’s difficulties/inconsistency)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch rightly press that founding-era intoxication laws were typically conduct-based and time-limited, not an always-on, status-based possession ban—so the Government cannot win by simply pointing to “intoxication” in the abstract. But under Bruen’s and Rahimi’s “relevantly similar” test (as Justice Alito and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize), the historical principle permits temporary disarmament tied to a present condition that makes armed possession unusually dangerous; that supports upholding § 922(g)(3) at least as applied where the Government proves active, ongoing unlawful use rather than remote or sporadic conduct. To meet the “how” mismatch Thomas identifies, our holding should be narrowly as-applied and should require contemporaneous, regular use (echoing Justice Jackson), avoiding any endorsement of an indeterminate disability untethered to present impairment-risk. That minimalist approach respects the Second Amendment’s historical inquiry while preserving institutional stability by deciding no more than necessary on this record.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed “narrow as-applied” approach still cannot supply the historical analogue Bruen requires, because the founding-era evidence he and Justice Alito invoke regulated carrying or firing while actually intoxicated or otherwise required a concrete, individualized basis for deeming someone dangerous. Recasting § 922(g)(3) as merely “temporary, condition-linked” disarmament does not solve the mismatch in “how”: the statute imposes an always-on possession ban keyed to an indeterminate status (“unlawful user”), not a time-of-impairment restriction or a judicially supervised dangerousness determination as in the historical tradition and as Rahimi’s analogical method presupposes. Justice Kagan’s reliance on Heller’s “presumptively lawful” dictum and “law-abiding” phrasing cannot do the Government’s historical work; to the extent that dictum is read to license broad status-based disarmament untethered to founding-era practice, it yields to the Second Amendment’s original public meaning. Administrability and the statute’s prevalence, emphasized by Justice Alito, are policy concerns that cannot override the Constitution’s text and history where the Government has not carried its burden on this record.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s central objection—that founding-era intoxication laws targeted only contemporaneous impairment and thus cannot justify an always-on status bar—has real force, but it assumes Bruen demands a near-identity in mechanism rather than a relevant similarity in “why” and “how.” As the Chief Justice notes, requiring proof of intoxication at the precise moment of possession would make § 922(g)(3) effectively unenforceable and would undercut the historically grounded principle that government may take prophylactic steps to prevent armed breaches of the peace by persons whose present condition makes misuse unusually likely. I agree with Justice Barrett and Justice Jackson that the indeterminacy concern is best handled by a narrowing, as-applied approach: the Government must prove active, ongoing unlawful use (or addiction) temporally connected to the possession, keeping the restriction temporary and condition-linked rather than an unbounded moral-status disability. Rahimi, properly read, does not replace history with free-floating risk analysis, but it does confirm that condition-based disarmament aimed at preventing special dangers of misuse can be consistent with the Second Amendment when the burden is comparably justified and comparably limited.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch are right to spotlight the mismatch between founding-era intoxication laws (moment-of-impairment) and § 922(g)(3)’s broader possession ban, but Bruen—as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize—asks for relevant similarity in “why” and “how,” not a historical carbon copy. The historically grounded principle is that government may prevent armed possession by people whose present condition makes misuse especially likely; regular, ongoing unlawful drug use can function as an administrable proxy for that same impairment-and-unreliability risk, consistent with Rahimi’s “special danger of misuse” framing. I agree with Justice Jackson that the indeterminacy concern must be addressed through an as-applied limitation requiring proof of contemporaneous, ongoing use (not stale or sporadic conduct), which keeps the law tied to current risk rather than a permanent moral-status disability. On that narrowed understanding, Thomas’s objection goes to overbreadth in particular applications, not facial invalidity on this record.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s and Justice Gorsuch’s strongest point—that founding-era intoxication laws regulate armed conduct only at the moment of impairment, while § 922(g)(3) can function as an always-on, status-based ban of indeterminate duration—squarely targets Bruen’s “how” requirement. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, Bruen (reinforced by Rahimi’s analogical method) asks for relevant similarity, not a historical twin, and the historical principle here is temporary disarmament keyed to a present condition of impaired judgment or heightened risk of misuse. The way to meet Thomas’s indeterminacy objection without converting the statute into an unworkable intoxication-at-the-instant-of-possession rule is to construe “unlawful user” (as Justice Jackson suggests) to require proof of current, ongoing unlawful use—a contemporaneous pattern that operates as an administrable proxy for the same impairment-and-danger rationale behind the historical restrictions. On that narrowed as-applied understanding, the statute’s burden is comparably justified and comparably limited, and I do not think Thomas’s critique undermines the Government’s showing under Bruen/Rahimi on this record.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I appreciate Chief Justice Roberts’s proposed narrowing move—upholding § 922(g)(3) only when the Government proves active, ongoing use—but that is not what the statute says, and it is not our role to rewrite an indeterminate status disability into a time-limited, conduct-linked restriction to make it comport with Bruen. Justice Alito’s and Justice Kagan’s appeal to “relevantly similar” analogues (intoxication and generalized dangerousness) still fails on Bruen’s own terms: those historical measures regulate possession or carrying during impairment or after an individualized predicate, whereas § 922(g)(3) imposes an always-on ban keyed to the vague category “unlawful user,” differing materially in both how it burdens the right and why it does so. Rahimi does not authorize a free-floating “special danger” standard untethered to representative historical analogues; it reaffirmed that history supplies the limits, not policy-driven administrability. If Congress wishes to target intoxicated carrying or provide a time-bounded, adjudication-linked disarmament regime, it may do so; but on this record and text, the Government has not carried its historical burden.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch make the best textual-historical objection: founding-era intoxication laws typically targeted carrying or use while actually impaired, whereas § 922(g)(3) can look like an indeterminate, status-based possession ban. But under Bruen—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Alito stress, and as Rahimi’s “why/how” framework confirms—the absence of a historical twin is not dispositive; the relevant tradition is condition-based, temporary disarmament to prevent predictable armed danger, and “current unlawful user/addict” can function (at least on this record) as an administrable proxy for ongoing impairment and unreliability. I agree with Justice Jackson that the indeterminacy concern requires a limiting principle: we should uphold the statute only as applied where the Government proves contemporaneous, regular unlawful use establishing a present-risk condition, rather than remote or sporadic use. That narrow path answers the strongest respondent-side critique without converting Bruen into a demand for moment-of-possession intoxication proof that would be historically underinclusive and practically unworkable.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Thomas and Justice Gorsuch press the hardest objection under Bruen: founding-era intoxication laws target armed conduct at the moment of impairment, while § 922(g)(3) can look like an indeterminate status-based possession ban. But as the Chief Justice notes, Bruen’s analogical inquiry is at the level of “relevantly similar” why/how, and a narrowing construction that requires proof of current, ongoing unlawful use (not remote or sporadic episodes) makes the law operate as a temporary, condition-linked disarmament—closer in kind to historical rules disarming those whose present condition makes firearms use unusually unsafe. Rahimi (highlighted by Justice Alito) strengthens, rather than weakens, that analysis by confirming that danger-based disarmament may rest on historically grounded principles even when modern legislatures use administrable proxies. I therefore would uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani, while making explicit that Thomas’s indeterminacy concern would have more force in applications lacking evidence of contemporaneous, regular use.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Thomas’s strongest objection—that founding-era intoxication laws were conduct-based at the moment of impairment and cannot justify an always-on, indeterminate status ban—squarely targets the Government’s weakest link: duration and nexus to present risk. But Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett persuasively show that Bruen’s (and Rahimi’s) analogue test is satisfied at an appropriate level of generality if—and only if—the statute is applied with a procedural limiting principle requiring proof of current, ongoing unlawful use that materially heightens the risk of unsafe gun handling, rather than remote or sporadic use. Justice Gorsuch’s separation-of-powers concern reinforces my view that we should not validate § 922(g)(3) as a free-floating moral-status disability; instead, courts must police the evidentiary predicate so the prohibition functions as a temporary, condition-linked restriction. On that narrowed as-applied understanding, the historical tradition of disarming those whose present condition makes them unsafe provides a sufficiently relevant analogue, and I would reverse the Fifth Circuit on this record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s analogical method, § 922(g)(3) can be sustained at least as applied to an active “unlawful user of” controlled substances because historical tradition supports temporarily disarming persons whose ongoing condition renders them unreliable or dangerous with arms, and founding- and 19th-century restrictions on firearms use while intoxicated are relevantly similar in justification and burden. Bruen does not require a dead-ringer historical twin, only a comparable justification and comparable burden, and it would be a significant and destabilizing step—given the statute’s widespread use and the acknowledged circuit conflict—to invalidate most applications of § 922(g)(3) on an as-applied record showing ongoing unlawful use. A narrow ruling upholding the statute as applied here preserves institutional legitimacy, avoids unnecessary constitutional breadth, and respects Congress’s judgment in targeting a class with heightened risk of impaired or irresponsible firearm use. The Fifth Circuit’s contrary approach reads Bruen too rigidly by demanding a precise founding-era analogue for modern drug-user disarmament rather than accepting historically grounded principles of disarming those whose condition undermines safe arms-bearing.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s text protects the right of “the people” to keep and bear arms, and under Bruen the Government must justify § 922(g)(3)’s categorical, status-based disarmament by pointing to a well-established historical analogue from the founding era or Reconstruction. The Government’s cited traditions—such as prohibitions on carrying or using firearms while intoxicated—regulate conduct at a time of impairment, not a broad, ongoing ban on mere status as an “unlawful user,” which can be temporally indeterminate and untethered to present dangerousness. Because § 922(g)(3) sweeps far beyond any historically grounded limitation and functions as a general disarmament of a disfavored class without an original-meaning pedigree, it violates the Second Amendment as applied to Hemani. Precedent to the contrary cannot control where it conflicts with the Constitution’s original public meaning and Bruen’s history-and-tradition framework.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Section 922(g)(3) fits within the Nation’s historical tradition of temporarily disarming persons whose condition makes them dangerous or unreliable with firearms, and Bruen does not demand a “historical twin” so long as the government identifies a relevantly similar analogue in both “why” and “how.” Under Rahimi’s application of Bruen’s analogical method, intoxication-and-dangerousness regulations (including laws restricting armed behavior while intoxicated and related peace-keeping measures) sufficiently support Congress’s judgment that active, unlawful drug use correlates with impaired judgment and heightened risk, justifying a categorical prohibition without requiring proof of contemporaneous intoxication at the moment of possession. Reading the Second Amendment to invalidate most applications of a widely used federal criminal statute would produce serious practical consequences for public safety and law enforcement, especially given Congress’s targeted focus on ongoing unlawful use or addiction rather than a one-time past act. Accordingly, as applied to Hemani, § 922(g)(3) is constitutional under the text-and-history framework of Bruen as clarified by Rahimi.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: As applied to Hemani, 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3) fits within the Constitution’s historically grounded acceptance of disarming persons whose condition makes firearm possession especially dangerous, and Bruen’s analogical method permits regulations that address the same public-safety problem even if they are not identical historical twins. Founding- and 19th-century restrictions on the use or carrying of firearms while intoxicated, and related dangerousness-based regulations, supply sufficiently similar “why” (preventing armed impairment and heightened risk) to justify temporarily disarming active unlawful drug users whose ongoing use correlates with impaired judgment and violence risk. Heller’s recognition that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited—and its assurance that “presumptively lawful” prohibitions on possession by certain categories (e.g., felons and the mentally ill) remain valid—supports Congress’s ability to adopt categorical, administrable disarmament rules for demonstrably risky statuses rather than requiring case-by-case dangerousness findings. The Fifth Circuit’s approach would unduly hamstring enforcement of a major federal public-safety statute and, in real-world operation, heighten risks to communities and vulnerable people harmed by gun violence.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s historical-analogue test, § 922(g)(3) is best understood as a permissible categorical judgment that habitual unlawful drug use is a condition associated with impaired judgment and heightened risk, akin to historical regulations restricting firearms use by those whose contemporaneous condition made them dangerous (including intoxication-related restrictions) and more general tradition-based limits on possession by non-“law-abiding, responsible citizens.” Heller’s repeated assurance that “longstanding prohibitions” on possession by certain categories (e.g., felons) are “presumptively lawful,” together with Bruen’s focus on the Second Amendment right as belonging to “law-abiding” citizens, leaves room for Congress to disarm a defined class whose ongoing unlawful conduct undermines responsible firearms use. As applied here, Congress may require firearms abstention for an “unlawful user of” controlled substances without proving intoxication at the moment of possession, because the statute targets a status defined by regular unlawful use rather than a one-off past act. Reversing avoids a regime in which § 922(g)(3) becomes largely unenforceable and supports a workable, administrable line consistent with the statute’s evident public-safety purpose and the Court’s Second Amendment precedents.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen, once the Second Amendment’s plain text covers an individual’s firearm possession, the government must justify § 922(g)(3) by demonstrating a historical tradition of comparable regulation; it has not shown a founding-era analogue for a categorical, status-based disarmament of persons merely because they are “unlawful user[s] of or addicted to” controlled substances, untethered to contemporaneous intoxication or an individualized finding of dangerousness. The proffered analogues—laws regulating arms use while intoxicated and more general “dangerousness” measures—do not match § 922(g)(3)’s “how” (a broad ban on possession at all times) or “why” (disarming based on a generalized status rather than a demonstrated, present risk) as Bruen requires. Separation-of-powers concerns counsel against allowing courts (or agencies via enforcement discretion) to expand historically accepted disarmament categories beyond those the Constitution’s original meaning permits. Accordingly, § 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied to Hemani absent proof tying his possession to intoxication or a historically grounded adjudication of dangerousness.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under Bruen’s historical-tradition inquiry, § 922(g)(3) is best understood as a modern analogue to long-accepted regulations temporarily disarming persons whose current condition makes firearm possession unusually dangerous or unreliable—most notably laws restricting carrying or using firearms while intoxicated—and to broader historical practices allowing legislatures to disarm categories of persons deemed dangerous. While the statute is status-based, it targets active “unlawful user[s]” or those “addicted to” controlled substances, which as applied can reasonably be treated as a proxy for ongoing impairment and heightened risk rather than a one-time past act. Given the significant federal reliance interests and the practical workability concerns of limiting the law only to moments of proven contemporaneous intoxication, I would uphold § 922(g)(3) at least as applied to Hemani and reverse the Fifth Circuit. This approach respects Bruen while adhering to judicial restraint and the Court’s longstanding recognition that the Second Amendment permits certain categorical restrictions consistent with history and tradition.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Second Amendment’s plain text presumptively covers Hemani’s possession of a firearm, so under Bruen the Government must show § 922(g)(3) is consistent with the Nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulation. Although founding-era history does not reveal a precise “historical twin” for disarming unlawful drug users, Bruen requires only a “well-established and representative historical analogue,” and the record of regulations disarming or restricting arms for those whose condition renders them dangerous or unreliable—especially intoxication-related carry/use restrictions and broader dangerousness-based disarmament—supports Congress’s judgment that active unlawful users of controlled substances pose an analogous risk. Properly understood, § 922(g)(3) targets a condition associated with impaired judgment and lawbreaking rather than imposing a freestanding moral-status disability, and that fit is sufficient under Bruen’s “why” and “how” analogical inquiry. Accordingly, I would reverse the Fifth Circuit and uphold § 922(g)(3) as applied to Hemani.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Applying Bruen’s framework, § 922(g)(3) can be upheld as applied where the government shows the defendant is a current, ongoing “unlawful user of or addicted to” controlled substances whose condition materially heightens the risk of unsafe firearm use, rather than merely pointing to a remote or sporadic use history. Rahimi confirms that legislatures may disarm categories of persons who present a “special danger of misuse,” and it permits reasoning at a level of generality that captures the principle—temporary or conditional disarmament tied to dangerousness—without demanding a Founding-era twin for modern drug-use status. Historical restrictions on weapon use while intoxicated and other danger-focused regulations are sufficiently “relevantly similar” in their why (preventing gun violence and accidents tied to impairment/unreliability) and how (limiting access/possession for those posing heightened risk), supporting Congress’s judgment in § 922(g)(3). To ensure procedural fairness, however, this application should require proof of contemporaneous, regular drug use establishing ongoing impairment risk, not an unbounded status-based prohibition untethered from practical dangerousness.
